newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic seen topping Bosnia poll - OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic seen topping Bosnia poll - OSCE.

text.p: Moslem leader Alija Izetbegovic is expected to win the contest to head Bosnia's joint presidency with most of the votes counted, figures released by international organisers showed on Wednesday.
Voters in Bosnia's first post-war election have also hoisted wartime Serb and Croat hardliners back into power with large majorities alongside Izetbegovic in the inter-ethnic presidency.
The election is the main plank of U.S.-led efforts to reintegrate the shattered country and mend deep wounds caused by ethnic cleansing, mass rape and massacre.
The 70-year-old Moslem leader looked almost certain to head the three-member executive by beating the leading Serb and Croat candidates Momcilo Krajisnik and Kresimir Zubak.

Both are nationalists who established unbeatable leads over their more moderate rivals. Izetbegovic's SDA party professes support for restoring a tolerant multi-ethnic Bosnia though critics see him as a Moslem nationalist hardliner.

The result means, under the Dayton peace agreement, that the 71-year-old former president of Bosnia will chair the joint executive, and represent Bosnia abroad. The presidency must govern by consensus.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said that with 86 out of 89 counting stations in the Moslem-Croat Federation reporting, Izetbegovic had 699,586 votes. His Bosnian Serb rival Momcilo Krajisnik had 631,767 votes from 59 out of 61 counting stations in the Serb Republic.

The OSCE figures showed Krajisnik's main challenger, moderate Mladen Ivanic, had taken 282,985 votes in a stronger than expected showing, while former prime minister Haris Silajdzic polled only 121,253 votes in the race for the Moslem seat.
Croat nationalist leader Zubak had polled 331,133 votes against 36,913 for rival Ivo Komsic in the fight for the Croat seat.
The OSCE said more than 1.2 million people had voted in the federation and 938,500 in the semi-autonomous Serb Republic, but cautioned some results were missing.

Despite Krajisnik's reputation as a hardline separatist, Western diplomats and Bosnian Serb sources said they expected him to cooperate in a new power-sharing arrangement designed to reintegrate Bosnia after 43 months of war.
Diplomats said Ivanic's strong showing was a backlash against Serb ultra-nationalists who tore Bosnia apart and got rich in war while most compatriots sank into penury.

Despite apparent resistance to the idea from hardline Serbs, Bosnia's outgoing Moslem-led republic government was confident U.S. pressure on the Serbs would ensure joint government got off the ground.
The United States said it would work with Bosnia's election victors over the next month or so, to set up joint governing bodies and then decide whether NATO forces should remain.
A 53,000-strong NATO-led force separated and demobilised Bosnia's factional armies early this year in a key pre-election step mandated by the Dayton treaty.
A team of OSCE-affiliated international observers has pronounced the elections free of serious irregularities in a preliminary report expected to lead to certification of the vote later this month.
